Spanish.summary: The most common home language of California English learners. Many English errors, like dropped final consonants, can reflect Spanish influence rather than a disorder.

sections.Sounds: Spanish has five vowel phonemes (/a e i o u/), while English has many more vowels, including many diphthongs, so English vowel pairs like "seat" and "sit" can be hard to tell apart. Spanish uses only five word-final consonants (/s, n, r, l, d/), so dropping final consonants or simplifying final clusters in English may reflect Spanish influence rather than a disorder. Spanish lacks or treats differently some English sounds, such as the "th" sounds and the "sh" versus "ch" contrast.
sections.Development: Across 27 languages, including Spanish, most consonants were acquired by age 5;0, and by 5;0 children produced at least 93% of consonants correctly. Plosives and nasals were acquired earlier than trills and flaps, so the Spanish trill may still be developing in young children.
sections.Language: In a study of 5-year-olds, Spanish-English bilingual children did not differ significantly from monolingual Spanish or English peers in segmental accuracy, syllabic accuracy, or phonological patterns, and cross-linguistic effects were limited. How much the child used each language did not predict phonological skills, so assess phonology directly in both languages. The sample was small (15 children).
sections.Assessment tools: Bilingual English-Spanish Assessment (BESA; Peña, Gutiérrez-Clellen, Iglesias, Goldstein, & Bedore), for ages 4;0 to 6;11. It has subtests given in both English and Spanish, plus parent and teacher questionnaires, and is designed to tell delays in English acquisition apart from true language disorders. Other Spanish speech tests include the Contextual Probes of Articulation Competence: Spanish (CPACS; Goldstein & Iglesias, 2006), the Bilingual Articulation Phonology Assessment: English/Spanish (BAPA; Fernandes, Kester, Bauman, & Prath, 2012), and the PLS-5 Spanish edition (Zimmerman, Steiner, & Pond, 2012).

Vietnamese.summary: Tonal language with three major dialects. Many English sound errors from Vietnamese speakers reflect first-language influence, not a disorder.

sections.Sounds: Vietnamese is a tonal language (6 tones are used in Viet Nam); English has no tones. There are three major dialects (Northern, Central, Southern) with different consonants, vowels, and tones, so ask the family which dialect the child speaks. English consonants not found in standard Vietnamese include /ɡ θ ð ʃ ʒ tʃ dʒ ɹ/ (sources differ slightly on /ɡ ʃ ʒ/, likely due to dialect), so errors on these in English may reflect first-language influence rather than a speech disorder.
sections.Development: Northern Vietnamese-speaking children had acquired nearly all Vietnamese sounds and tones by about age 5;5 to 5;11. Exceptions were initial /ɲ, s, z, x/, the semivowel /w/ within syllables, and tones 3 (ngã) and 4 (hỏi), so errors on these may still be typical before age 6. This study covered the Northern dialect only.
sections.Language: In a 4-year study of school-age Vietnamese-English children in the US, both languages grew, but English grew faster, so many children shifted toward English dominance, and receptive and expressive skills followed different patterns. Lower Vietnamese skills compared to English may reflect this shift, not a disorder. Parents' use of Vietnamese supported children's Vietnamese vocabulary and did not slow their English vocabulary.
sections.Assessment tools: Vietnamese Speech Assessment (Phạm, Le, & McLeod, 2016); Multilingual Assessment Instrument for Narratives (MAIN), Vietnamese version; Intelligibility in Context Scale (ICS), Vietnamese version.

Mandarin.summary: Tonal language. Children in Hua & Dodd (2000) acquired tones first and syllable-initial consonants last.

sections.Development: In Hua and Dodd's study of Putonghua (Modern Standard Chinese), children acquired tones first, and tone errors were uncommon. Syllable-final consonants and vowels came next, and syllable-initial consonants came last. Initial consonant acquisition was complete by 3;6 for 75% of children. By 4;6, children produced initial consonants correctly about two-thirds of the time, except four affricates. Weak stress and the rhotacized feature were not fully acquired in the oldest children studied.
sections.Across languages: Across 27 languages, including Mandarin (Putonghua), most consonants were acquired by age 5;0, and by 5;0 children produced at least 93% of consonants correctly.
sections.Ask the family: Mandarin and Cantonese are different languages. When a family says the child speaks "Chinese," ask which language, since development research and tests differ.
sections.Assessment tools: Putonghua Segmental Phonology Test (PSPT; So & Zhou, 2000). Picture-naming task for Putonghua (Hua, 2002). Mandarin Phonology Test with a Nonlinear Scan Analysis form (Zhao & Bernhardt, 2012).

sources: Hua, Z., & Dodd, B. (2000). The phonological acquisition of Putonghua (Modern Standard Chinese). Journal of Child Language, 27(1), 3-42. https://doi.org/10.1017/S030500099900402X

Arabic.summary: Children speak a spoken dialect at home and learn Standard Arabic mainly at school. Ask which variety the child speaks and which one a test uses.

sections.Diglossia: Arabic-speaking children grow up speaking Spoken Arabic for everyday talk at home and in the neighborhood. Standard Arabic is used for reading, writing, and formal settings like the classroom, so children first learn to read in a variety they do not speak. Tasks in Standard Arabic may measure the child's familiarity with that variety, not only the skill the task targets.
sections.Development: In a study of 180 Jordanian Arabic-speaking children aged 2;0 to 6;4, ages of consonant acquisition and mastery were similar to English, with notable exceptions. Medial consonants were more accurate than initial and final consonants. Across 27 languages, including Arabic, most consonants were acquired by age 5;0.
sections.Dialects: Arabic speech research comes from specific countries and dialects, including Jordanian, Egyptian, Kuwaiti, and Lebanese Arabic. Ask the family which dialect the child speaks, and match research and tests to that dialect when possible.
sections.Assessment tools: Mansoura Arabic Articulation Test (MAAT; Abou-Elsaad, Baz, & El-Banna, 2009), based on Egyptian Arabic. Kuwaiti Arabic Phonology Test (Ayyad, Bernhardt, & Stemberger, 2012). Amayreh Articulation Test (Amayreh & Dyson, 1998), based on Jordanian Arabic, and its modified version (Hamdan & Amayreh, 2007). Match the test to the child's dialect when possible.

Cantonese.summary: Tonal language. Children in So & Dodd (1995) mastered tones and vowels by age 2 and made few phonological errors after age 4.

sections.Development: So and Dodd found that Cantonese-speaking children had mastered the contrastive use of tones and vowels by age 2. The order of consonant acquisition was similar to English. Developmental error patterns were also common in other languages, and some error patterns specific to Cantonese were identified. Few phonological errors occurred after age 4.
sections.Across languages: Across 27 languages, including Cantonese, most consonants were acquired by age 5;0, and by 5;0 children produced at least 93% of consonants correctly.
sections.More research: Cantonese tone development: Mok, Li, and Fung (2020). Cantonese consonant development: Wong and Stokes (2001).
sections.Assessment tools: Hong Kong Cantonese Articulation Test (HKCAT; Cheung, Ng, & To, 2006). Cantonese Segmental Phonology Test (So, 1993). Cantonese Phonological Assessment Guideline (So, 1992). Hong Kong Cantonese Tone Identification Test (Lee, 2010).

sources: So, L. K. H., & Dodd, B. J. (1995). The acquisition of phonology by Cantonese-speaking children. Journal of Child Language, 22(3), 473-495. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305000900009922
